background.definition: An idiopathic condition most common in children causing osteonecrosis of the femoral head.

list.listitem: Incidence in children under 15 years old varies by race, geographic, and socioeconomic factors from 0.2 to 19.1/100,000/year.
The majority of cases are unilateral, with bilateral involvement reported in 10% to 15% of cases.
Males are affected at a ratio of 5:1 over females, although bilateral cases are more common in females.
The highest incidence is reported in whites and lower socioeconomic status.

Legg-Calve-Perthes disease occurs in approximately 2.7% of children diagnosed with transient synovitis of the hip, with a prevalence of 36.3% in those with recurrent or persisten symptoms, highlighting the importance of targeted follow-up x-rays after 6 weeks
Felt to be multifactorial, yet etiology remains unclear.
Osteonecrosis is thought to be due to a disruption of blood flow and bone resorption during growth.
Micro-trauma, environmental conditions, prenatal insults, genetic factors, or hypercoagulability status may contribute, but no causal link has been firmly demonstrated.
A similar ischemic condition was created in piglet studies through induction of avascular necrosis by ligating femoral vasculature.
Idiopathic ischemia to the femoral head causes vascular compromise during growth, resulting in a mismatch of bone metabolism with increased resorption and delayed formation.
The ischemic femoral head fragments under repetitive mechanical loading and a deformity occurs.
Blood flow returns to normal within 2 to 4 years following the avascular period.
The femoral head deformity may cause progressive damage to the hip joint leading the patient to develop arthritis, femoroacetabular impingement, and osteochondritis dissecans.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Geographic location – increased risk with every 10° latitude increase from equator

list.listitem: No screening guidelines exist. C
Patients with Factor V Leiden have a 3 times greater likelihood of developing LCPD, but this only explains 3% of cases. C

Consider Legg-Calve-Perthes disease (LCPD) in a child that presents with a limp, hip pain, referred pain to the knee, limited range of motion in hip abduction and internal rotation, or antalgic gait. C
Obtain plain AP and frog lateral view pelvic radiographs of both femoral heads on all patients suspected of having LCPD; consider MRI or bone scan when plain films are non-diagnostic. C
Laboratory studies including CBC, ESR, and CRP may help exclude similarly presenting conditions. C
Suspect LCPD in a child with a painless limp, especially after exertion, or a limp with pain in the groin, hip, thigh, or knee. It is most commonly diagnosed between the ages of 4 and 8 years.

Patients often have decreased range of motion in abduction and internal rotation on exam, and an antalgic or Trendelenburg gait (dropping of the pelvis and shortened step on the unaffected side of the body during heel strike of the affected side).
Children are often small for their age with delayed bone age.
Depending on the length of time between symptom onset and presentation, the child may have muscle atrophy of the affected leg, hip muscle contracture, and a leg-length discrepancy.
Patients with chronic LCPD may present with a history of pain for weeks.
Laboratory studies including CBC, ESR, and CRP help clinicians exclude infectious and inflammatory causes of hip pain.

Imaging is the mainstay of diagnosis, classification, and follow-up. When LCPD is suspected, AP and frog lateral views of the pelvis should be obtained early. When bilateral hip involvement is present, radiographs show each hip in different stages of disease progression and can help to distinguish between other conditions.
Initial plain films can be normal for the first 3 to 6 months, so if there is a high index of suspicion, clinicians could progress to ordering a bone scan or MRI.
CT may be used for early diagnosis of bone collapse and to identify interosseous changes later in LCPD, but is limited by the high dose of radiation.
Diffusion weighted MRI without gadolinium may predict hip prognosis by analyzing metaphyseal and epiphyseal diffusion coefficients.
MRI with gadolinium gives a clearer picture of the involved area of the femoral epiphysis.
Ultrasonography findings are nonspecific but may help differentiate LCPD from transient synovitis.
Radiographic changes in LCPD are commonly classified by the Herring (prognostic), Catterall (prognostic), and/or Stulberg (outcome) classification systems.

The Herring classification system () uses the lateral pillar of the femoral head to categorize LCPD, is the most common system used, correlates best with final outcome, and has the best interobserver reliability.
The Catterall classification system () describes the relationship between femoral head involvement in LCPD during the fragmentation stage and patient outcome.
The Stulberg radiographic classification () assesses the effectiveness of treatment; the femoral head deformity class determines the likelihood of long-term sequelae of LCPD after skeletal maturity.
Suspect LCPD in a limping child with no clear mechanism of injury or a child with thigh or referred knee pain.
Consider early plain films if there is a high index of suspicion and progress to MRI or bone scan if radiographs are negative for early-stage presentation.
Children diagnosed with LCPD should be referred to a pediatric orthopedic surgeon for management. C
Treatment focuses on containing the femoral head within the acetabulum through the use of nonoperative or operative methods. C
Evidence to determine the best mode of treatment of LCPD is very limited. Treatment approaches are largely based on preference, experience, and training of orthopedic surgeons. B
Anti-inflammatories should be used when synovitis is present.

Bisphosphonates have been shown to delay necrotic bone resorption without enhancing anabolism in animal models. Bisphosphonates have been used to treat LCPD and maintain Z scores but their benefit in humans is unproven.
Surgical containment is achieved by an osteotomy of the femur and/or innominates. Proximal femoral varus osteotomy is one of the most widely used operative procedures.

A meta-analysis of 50 articles, most of which were prospective cohort studies, case series, and case controls, compared nonoperative and operative approaches to treatment but the evidence was inconclusive due to heterogeneity and conflicting results. Most treatment approaches were found to be based on preference, experience, and training of clinicians.

Results comparing different surgical interventions were inconclusive, but innominate osteotomy may offer improved angular positioning, minimized scarring, and less possibility of introducing limb shortening based largely on small cohort studies and case series.

The Perthes Study Group led a multicenter prospective observational study of 438 patients aged 6 to 12 years with LCPD. All were classified in either a non-operative group (no treatment, brace treatment, range-of-motion exercises) or an operative group (femoral osteotomy, innominate osteotomy). There were no differences in outcome between treatments in the non-operative group and also in comparison with the operative group. Three prognostic conclusions were drawn: 1) children with symptoms prior to 8 years old were likely to have good results regardless of treatment; 2) in children with onset greater than 8 and at least 50% lateral pillar height maintenance (Herring Groups B and B/C), operative groups had better results; and 3) patients with greater than 50% collapse of the lateral pillar height (Herring Group C) had poor outcome regardless of treatment.

Researchers identified a cohort of 30 children (36 hips) with LCPD diagnosed prior to age 5 and reviewed their hips at skeletal maturity. Over 50% were in Catterall Group III or IV and Herring Group C, and at maturity only 45% had a good outcome according to the Stulberg classification, while 22% had poor and 33% fair outcomes.

In a series of 51 children older than 8 years with severe LCPD, results of shelf acetabuloplasty was evaluated. The authors reported good outcomes, an improved Iowa hip score and normal passive range of motion of the hip.

In a case report of a 12-year-old patient with a poor prognosis, the patient was noted to have improved pain after 30 sessions of needle and laser acupuncture on the hip joint, and after 196 sessions he had a full recovery.

One of the most common recommended nonoperative therapies for LCPD is non-weight bearing of the affected limb with crutches, but this is controversial. While some clinical studies have shown a benefit with prolonged bed rest and cast immobilization, others have not.
Physical therapy with active and passive range of motion of the hip and knee may help maintain joint mobility, along with adductor stretching, but has not been studied in clinical trials.
Early nonoperative treatment focused on complete non-weight bearing and the use of bed rest or a wheelchair.
Short-term Petrie casting in a position of abduction and internal rotation popularized abduction casting with weight bearing and helped stretch adductors for increased range of motion.

Removable braces that mimic Petrie casting (Atlanta, Toronto, Newington braces) have replaced casting but no benefit has been seen with these over observation and range-of-motion exercises of the hip.

When combined with core decompression for osteonecrosis of the femoral head, autologous bone marrow stem cell therapy at 12 and 24 months had more favorable pain relief, Harris hip scores and delayed the collapse of the femoral head.

Bone marrow stem cell therapy reduces the risk of femoral head collapse (OR = 0.15) and conversion to total hip arthroplasty (OR = 0.20), while improving functional outcomes (Harris hip score MD = 10.7) and reducing pain in patients with early-stage avascular necrosis of the hip, suggesting that when combined with core decompression it may offer a more effective treatment option compared to conventional methods.
Consultation with a pediatric orthopedic surgeon is recommended at diagnosis given the complexities of treatment.
LCPD is a self-healing disorder.
The aim of treatment is to prevent development of complications such as irregular contouring of the femoral head, shortening of the femoral neck, or flattening of the vertical wall of the acetabulum.
Development of any hip deformities can result in osteoarthritis at an early age.
Short- and long-term prognosis of LCPD can be good but depends on the level of femoral head deformity present. C
Children presenting with symptoms prior to 5 years to 8 years of age typically have a better prognosis than children presenting with symptoms later in life. B

LCPD is a self-healing condition in which blood supply returns to the capital femoral epiphysis spontaneously by either rapid recanalization of existing vessels occurring within weeks or the formation of new vessels within a period of months to years.
The prognosis of LCPD can be good but depends on the involvement of the epiphyseal center, femoral head, subsequent healing, and proper joint space preservation.

Short-term prognosis correlates with femoral head deformity at the end of the healing stage. Risk factors affecting short-term prognosis include onset at an older age, extensive femoral epiphyseal involvement, femoral head containment, reduced range of motion in the hip, and premature closure of the growth plate.

Long-term prognosis correlates with the potential to develop osteoarthritis of the hip as an adult. In a prospective study of 59 patients, 60 hips were diagnosed with LCPD between 1959 and 1974. Forty-two of these 60 hips were Catterall type 2 or 3. In 2002, 33 hips had Catterall type 2 or 3 and 12/33 hips (36%) had signs of osteoarthritis. In 2010, 27 hips were re-evaluated and 15/27 (55%) had signs of osteoarthritis, showing that osteoarthritis was prevalent between the 4th and 5th decades of life.
With proper rest, symptom resolution occurs in most patients within 24 to 36 months and monitoring should be continued until reossification of the femoral head occurs.

Class I – normal hip joint
Good/no arthritis

Good/no arthritis

Fair/mild-to-moderate arthritis

Poor/moderate arthritis

Bad/severe early arthritis before 50 yo
